title: Winter Car Emergency Gear: Portable Jump Starters and Tire Inflators Explained
subtitle: How a portable battery pack and a small air pump can help in a cold-weather jam, and what each one cannot do.
excerpt: Cold weather weakens car batteries and lowers tire pressure. Here is how portable jump starters and tire inflators work, why no independent source gave a charging schedule, and what else belongs in your trunk this winter.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Few things are as discouraging as a cold morning, a full day of errands ahead, and a car that only clicks when you turn the key. Winter is hard on cars. Consumer Reports notes that a 12-volt car battery has only about half its cranking power at 0°F compared with 80°F. Consumer Reports also notes that cold air lowers the pressure in your tires.

Two small gadgets can help: a portable jump starter, which can restart a car with a weak battery without needing a second car, and a portable tire inflator, which pumps air back into a low tire. Consumer Reports suggests carrying a portable jump starter. Neither gadget replaces a mechanic or roadside assistance, but both can help in a pinch.

A jump starter is a rechargeable battery pack with a pair of jumper clamps attached. You connect the clamps to your car battery, turn the unit on, and start the car. Follow the maker's manual for exactly where the clamps go and in what order. Many models add safety features. "Spark-proof" means the connections are designed not to spark, and "reverse polarity protection" means the unit guards against damage if the clamps are attached the wrong way around.

Makers rate these packs in "peak amps," a measure of the burst of power they can deliver. Those ratings are measured at room temperature, and cold changes things. In an older Consumer Reports test, most units started a weak battery at room temperature, yet when both the battery and the jump starter were at 0°F, the report found that "none of the units were able to jump start even the weak car batteries." Consumer Reports says it no longer tests or updates this category, so treat the findings as a useful warning rather than current ratings. It also found that a higher price did not predict better performance.

A tire inflator is a small air pump. Some run on a rechargeable battery and some on 12-volt car power. Many let you set a target pressure, then stop when the tire reaches it. They are handy for topping up tires that went soft in the cold. For a nail or a real puncture, though, Roberto Baldwin of Reviewed puts it simply: "inflation is only a temporary fix." You will still need a tire shop. Expect some noise, too. In Reviewed's tests, the Avid Power 20V cordless inflator was the loudest tested, at 89.5 decibels.

items: Match the size to your car. A very powerful jump starter is better suited to trucks, SUVs and larger engines. A smaller car does not need the biggest model.

Check the weight and the grip. Clamps and hose connections need a firm grip. This is our suggestion, not a sourced finding: squeeze them in the store if you can, or ask a family member to try them. If you have limited grip or lifting strength, look for a lighter unit with a simple clamp design.
Look for an automatic shut-off on inflators, so you can set the pressure and step back instead of watching a gauge.
Watch for hidden costs. Reviewed lists the DeWalt DCC020IB inflator as sold with the battery separate, and says the battery for the Black & Decker BDINF20C costs extra.

Make sure accessories are in the box. One customer review of the One Smart inflator on Home Depot's page says accessories were missing. That is a single anecdote, but it is worth checking what is included.
Measure your trunk. Reviewed says the DeWalt DCC020IB is large and not suited to compact cars. We could not confirm its current price.
Check the retailer's return policy before you buy.

sections.content: If you would rather spend less on an inflator, AutoZone's category page listed several basic models in November 2026, including a Slime 40059 tire air compressor kit at $21.49 with pickup. That is a listing price, not a product page we read, so check current price and details before you buy.
Setting it up and keeping it ready

A jump starter only helps if it is charged. No independent source we read gave a recharge schedule, so read the manual for how often the maker suggests topping it up. Setting a reminder on your calendar or phone is our suggestion.

Where you store it matters. Consumer Reports advises keeping jump starters out of direct sun, in the glovebox or trunk. The tested units had storage limits from 120°F to 185°F, and Consumer Reports cites NHTSA figures showing a parked car in the sun can reach 131°F to 172°F. So check the storage limits in your unit's manual, especially in a hot trunk.

Round out your trunk with the basics Consumer Reports recommends: gloves, a blanket, a shovel, an ice scraper, a flashlight, flares or a reflective triangle, a first aid kit and a phone. Consumer Reports also advises keeping your gas tank at least half full and having your car battery tested.

A jump starter and tire inflator are tools, not a rescue service. They cannot call for help, and they may not work in deep cold. The Consumer Reports cold test was older and is no longer updated. We found no independent cold-weather rating for either product below, and the NOCO GB30 results in that older test should not be applied to the GB150. Keep a roadside assistance number in your phone, and if you feel unsafe, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A little preparation goes a long way in winter. A charged jump starter, a simple air pump and a well-stocked trunk can turn a stressful morning into a smaller problem.

products.name: NOCO Boost Pro GB150 3000A Lithium Jump Starter
products.blurb: Suits trucks, SUVs, RVs and larger engines; rated for gas engines up to 9.0L and diesel up to 7.0L, which is more capacity than a typical car needs. It has spark-proof connections, reverse polarity protection and a built-in light. Weight, size and warranty were not confirmed on the page, and no independent source gives a cold-weather rating for it.

products.name: OATI-001L 11.1V Cordless Tire Inflator
products.blurb: A compact cordless pump for drivers who want to top up tires without plugging in. You set the pressure and it stops on its own, and it has a built-in USB power bank. Weight was not confirmed on the page, and one customer review says accessories were missing, so check the box.

products.name: RoadBoost 4-in-1 Roadside Emergency Kit
products.blurb: One compact unit that jump-starts a dead battery without a second car, inflates a low tire to a PSI you set and then stops by itself, and doubles as an emergency light and phone charger.
